title: Kubernetes observability-first boot + upgrade checklist for on-prem mixed infra
content:
Purpose
This is a practical, observability-first runbook for bootstrapping and performing safe upgrades of on-prem Kubernetes clusters across mixed infrastructure (bare metal + vSphere). It intentionally flips the usual sequence: instrument and validate telemetry before risky state changes. That reduces unknowns during upgrades and makes postmortems actionable.

Scope and assumptions
- Target clusters: 1. small staging fleets (3 control-plane + 3 worker) and 2. production fleets (HA control plane across vSphere or baremetal with separate worker racks).
- We assume Terraform manages foundational infra and an operator (or templated manifests) handles cluster resources.
- Air-gapped and restricted networks: include notes for artifact staging.
- Rolling upgrade strategy preferred; rollback is only for limited failure classes.

High-level flow
1) Preflight (observability-first)
   - Verify metrics, logs, and traces are collected and can be queried before making changes.
   - Validate that synthetic probes and SLI dashboards exist for critical control-plane and kubelet health.
   - Snapshot current state: kube-apiserver logs, etcd leader history, control-plane resource usage, Pod Disruption Budgets (PDBs).
2) Terraform plan and immutable artifacts
   - Run terraform plan and store plan JSON for audit.
   - Lock module versions and store the module commit sha with the plan.
3) Canary / smoke nodes in staging
   - Apply to a small canary pool with identical topology (same NIC driver/kernel).
   - Observe metrics and alerts for 30-60 minutes.
4) Gradual rollout to production
   - Node-by-node drain, upgrade, validate; or control-plane rolling replacement where required.
   - Maintain at least 2 healthy control-plane instances during upgrades.

Preflight checklist (detailed)
- Observability checks (must pass before upgrade)
  - Metrics: prometheus targets for etcd, kube-apiserver, kube-controller-manager, kube-scheduler, kubelet. Confirm scrape success rate > 99% over 5m.
  - Logs: central logging ingestion test. Execute a synthetic log emission and confirm it appears within retention window.
  - Traces: basic end-to-end trace for API server request latency. Run a sample request and observe trace in tracing UI.
  - Alerts: silence non-essential alerts for the maintenance window but keep SLO breach alerts active. Ensure alert routing to oncall.
- Inventory & baselines
  - List nodes with kernel version, NIC model, BIOS/firmware, container runtime, kubelet version, kube-proxy mode.
  - Baseline: capture 1h average p95 pod startup time, apiserver p95 latency, etcd leader election frequency.
- Backups
  - etcd snapshot: perform snapshot, copy to off-cluster storage, verify restore process in staging.
  - Terraform state: ensure remote backend is healthy and state is locked before changes.
- Artifact staging for air-gapped environments
  - Stage images and operator manifests into local registry. Verify checksums.
  - For vSphere OVA/iso: store checksums and verify SHA256 on target appliance.

Terraform module notes (practical specifics)
- Modules should expose these variables: control_plane_count, worker_count_per_rack, ssh_pubkeys, mtu, os_image_ref, kube_version, container_runtime_version, node_labels, node_taints. Keep defaults conservative.
- Outputs required: control_plane_ips, worker_node_names, ignition_url (for baremetal), vsphere_vm_template (for vSphere flows).
- State handling: use separate state files for control-plane vs worker pools to make partial applies safer. Locking: use DynamoDB/Consul or GCS bucket locks depending on backend.
- Idempotency: design modules so that reprovisioning a node is possible without changing cluster identity (e.g., preserve node names or use a node registration token).
- Upgrade knobs: expose kubelet_version and kubeadm_config_template as module variables, not as inline hacks.

Observability-specific Terraform/infra advice
- Create a minimal logging/metrics forwarding stack as part of the bootstrap: node-exporter, cadvisor, kube-state-metrics, fluentd/lf.
- Deploy a small load-generator or synthetic probe DaemonSet that can run simple workloads and report to tracing. Keep it enabled on canaries only.

Upgrade procedure: control plane first (preferred)
- Step 0: announce maintenance, ensure oncall and SRE present.
- Step 1: roll out new control-plane VM/template to 1 canary control-plane node. If vSphere, bring up OVA clone; if baremetal, reprovision PXE with new ignition.
- Step 2: join canary control-plane, wait for etcd sync and confirm quorum. Watch etcd leader and member health.
- Step 3: run full acceptance suite: control-plane API smoke, scheduler failover, leader change. Confirm no increase in 5m apiserver latency.
- Step 4: roll remaining control-plane nodes one at a time. Do not reduce control-plane quorum below 3 in prod.

Worker upgrades
- Cordon + drain with a small grace period and force if necessary only after validation. Prefer kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --pod-selector 'app!=system-probe'.
- Replace node via Terraform when immutable reprovisioning is used. For in-place kubelet upgrades, follow kubeadm recommended sequence.

Rollback vs Rollforward guidance
- Prefer rollforward where possible: if a version causes pod failures, deploy fixes or increase rollback window for the offending workloads. Rollback of control-plane is risky due to etcd and CRD state changes.
- If rollback is necessary, ensure you have etcd snapshot taken immediately before control-plane change and tested restore in staging.

Common failure modes and remediation heuristics
- Kubelet failing after kernel upgrade: check dmesg for driver mismatch, revert to previous kernel via image/ PXE tag or reprovision.
- NICs flapping after firmware change: verify firmware image, rollback firmware if available, or move node to maintenance and replace with known-good hardware.
- CRD conversion errors post-upgrade: ensure CRD conversion webhooks are available and roll forward CRD conversion controllers; if webhook unavailable, pause upgrade.
- Network plugin incompatibility: keep CNI version pinned in module and test in staging with same MTU and overlay settings.

Air-gapped specifics
- Push container images and Helm charts to private registry with tags: module_version+cluster_digest. Record checksums.
- Provide a local package server for kubeadm/kubelet binaries.

Runbook drills and post-upgrade validation (observability-first play)
- Immediately after each node/control-plane change: verify monitoring targets are healthy, logging ingestion latency within baseline, and traces appear for synthetic probes.
- Execute a smoke checklist: list pods in CrashLoopBackOff, DNS resolution checks from a worker pod, sample inference call to a representative model service.
- Post-upgrade KPI review: token-cost telemetry for inference rarely changes, but latency/timeout regressions are critical. Tag the deployment with the terraform plan sha and kubelet version for audit.

Small utilities and checks (examples)
- check-kernel-mods.sh (to run on node)
  - uname -r; lsmod | grep -E 'ixgbe|i40e|bcm'; dmesg | tail -n 50
- quick-etcd-health.sh
  - kubectl get --raw '/healthz?verbose' | jq '.' || kubectl -n kube-system logs -l component=etcd

Open questions / follow-ups
- Convert the monitoring smoke suite into a Canary operator that can be toggled via labels.
- Evaluate moving to immutable control-plane templates with ignition that preserves etcd data disk mapping.
- Document a tested etcd restore for production with step-by-step recovery and time estimates.

Appendix: useful links and tickets
- Confluence: Private Deployments Observability Primer (linked above)
- Terraform modules repo: github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-modules (see PR 128 for ignition/template changes)
- Tickets: JIRA-PRJ-4312 (upgrade cadence proposal), JIRA-OPS-3891 (airgap staging gaps)

Notes to self
- Keep this document short and actionable; move deep-dive diagnostic commands into a separate diagnostics notebook.
- Schedule a 2-hour upgrade dry run in staging with SRE and the applied-ml team present.
